profile.reading: Per DC BLOX own site, this Birmingham, Alabama facility sits at 433 6th Street South and currently operates 31,000 square feet, supporting up to 5 MW of critical load today and expandable to 60 MW; DC BLOX has published expansion plans totaling 263,000 square feet and 49 critical MW committed and planned for large scale deployments. The facility holds Uptime Institute Tier III Certification of Constructed Facility, meaning it is concurrently maintainable with no shutdowns required for equipment maintenance or replacement. DC BLOX operates a network of data centers across the Southeast United States; per the company's own data center map page, it operates 23 facilities totaling 2,780,376 square feet and 470 critical MW company-wide, of which this Birmingham facility and its planned 263,000-square-foot, 49-critical-MW expansion represent one component. Birmingham's downtown core has drawn colocation and enterprise IT investment as Alabama's largest metro, with this facility positioned to serve as a regional interconnection point distinct from DC BLOX's coastal Myrtle Beach cable landing station and its smaller Chattanooga facility, both tracked elsewhere in this registry. No year-opened date was located for this facility in sourcing reachable this session. The facility's expansion figures (263,000 sq ft, 49 critical MW) reflect committed and planned capacity per the operator's own site rather than currently built-out space, a distinction this entry preserves rather than treats as already operational. DC BLOX positions itself as a regional Southeast US colocation and network fabric provider rather than a national hyperscale operator, emphasizing secondary and tertiary metro markets (Birmingham, Chattanooga, Huntsville, Charleston, and Myrtle Beach among them) that larger national operators have historically underserved, a strategy distinct from the dense Northern Virginia or Silicon Valley clustering seen among many other operators tracked in this registry.

reading.body:
DC BLOX Birmingham represents more than half of Alabama's publicly disclosed data center power at 5 MW today, with expansion plans to 49 MW, but the state's AI infrastructure visibility remains severely limited.

The facility's current footprint of 31,000 square feet supports roughly 625 racks at conservative density. Expansion plans to 263,000 square feet and 49 MW would support approximately 6,100 racks. Only two of twelve mapped facilities in Alabama publish power figures, meaning the state's actual data center capacity is largely unknown. This lack of transparency obscures whether Alabama is building infrastructure for AI or other workloads.

The 10-fold expansion ratio from current to planned capacity signals committed growth, but expansion alone does not determine whether this facility serves AI scaling. Tenant type and network connectivity are not published. The binding constraint on DC BLOX Birmingham's relevance to AI is not its specifications but whether Alabama's regional power grid and backhaul can absorb 49 MW of demand at full buildout and route that traffic efficiently to where computation occurs.

Tier III certification ensures the facility can undergo maintenance without shutdown, a technical requirement for reliability-sensitive workloads. This does not indicate what workloads will occupy the space or when capacity will fill.
